old: This chapter explains how a Caro position can be represented, tested for a result, evaluated and searched. It connects the concepts to evidence from the project while distinguishing three implementation contexts. The current application controller and frontend rules can be inspected directly in the application source. The repository's source excerpts and baseline modules document the core Rust engine functions, state representations, and search procedures used by the WebAssembly package [6]. Together with the compiled WebAssembly binary and TypeScript adapter contracts, these artifacts specify the active engine behavior and its boundary with the frontend controller [6], [7], [9].
new: This chapter develops the board representation, terminal rule, evaluation function and search algorithms used in the Caro project. The current frontend and its Worker adapter are examined alongside two research implementations: the modified Rust engine recorded in the 23 October source snapshot [6], and the separate native reference engine [8]. The active application calls a vendored WebAssembly package through the request interface and Worker adapter [3], [9], [26]. These sources have different roles: frontend source establishes request and commit behavior, Rust source explains the recorded algorithm, and binary execution establishes the behavior of the tested package.
reason: Separates source ownership and binary execution; removes unsupported claim that old baseline plus adapter establishes active binary internals.

old: A position consists of 225 cells, each containing empty, X or O. In an array indexed as B[y][x], row-major conversion to a flat logical index is i = 15y + x; the inverse is x = i mod 15, y = floor(i/15). Hence the center (7,7) has index 112, and (14,14) has index 224. The system divides board representation across three specialized structures according to architectural role: (1) the Rust search engine (Board) stores a contiguous 15 × 15 grid of 225 one-byte repr(u8) cells (Empty = 0, Black = 1, White = 2) paired with move_count; (2) the match wrapper (Game) and frontend (GameState) store match progression and an ordered Move history; and (3) the legacy TypeScript bot (BotBoard) uses a 1D sentinel-padded array with directional bitmask segments. The rationale for this division is to decouple high-frequency recursive search from match-lifecycle management. Its primary benefit is O(1) direct indexing, O(1) in-place apply/undo during depth-first search, zero per-node heap allocation, and compact L1-cache locality; the trade-off is that the raw 225-cell matrix does not record chronological move order, requiring the outer Game/GameState layer to maintain history and full-board unindexed scans to take O(N²) time [13].
new: A position contains 225 cells, each empty, X or O. For a logical matrix B[y][x], row-major conversion is i = 15y + x, with inverse x = i mod 15 and y = floor(i/15). The center (7,7) therefore has index 112, and (14,14) has index 224. In the modified Rust source, Board stores a 15 × 15 array of repr(u8) cells and a move counter. Its cell values are Empty = 0, Black = 1 and White = 2; the array occupies 225 bytes, while the complete Board also contains the counter and any alignment padding [6], [13]. The frontend GameState instead stores occupied coordinates in a Map and maintains ordered move history [14]. The legacy BotBoard uses a one-dimensional array padded with boundary sentinels. These representations support different operations: direct Rust cell access, frontend match history, and incremental line analysis in the legacy bot.
reason: Corrects frontend Map representation; removes false zero-per-node-allocation and unmeasured L1-cache claims; distinguishes cell array from struct size.

old: The archived Rust place excerpt validates bounds, rejects an empty stone, rejects an occupied cell, writes a cell and increments a move counter. The companion undo rejects an out-of-range or already-empty cell and otherwise clears it and decrements that counter [6]. Dividing responsibility between low-level cell mutation (Board::place and Board::undo) and match-level legality (Game::play_move and GameController) keeps inner-loop search operations lightweight while ensuring that turn alternation and post-win lockouts are strictly enforced on committed game moves.
new: In the modified Rust snapshot, Board::place checks bounds, rejects an empty stone or occupied cell, writes the stone and increments move_count. Board::undo rejects an invalid or empty coordinate, then clears the occupied cell and decrements the counter [6]. These operations maintain the position. Turn alternation, move history and terminal lockout belong to the Rust Game wrapper and the frontend match controller, rather than to Board::place itself [2].
reason: The checked undo and empty-stone rejection are modified-source behavior, absent from old baseline; describes legality owners without universal guarantee.

old: A board and a game are different state owners. Cells and the count describe the position; turn, winner, and move history describe the match's progression. A history provides the information needed to restore actual game moves in reverse order. A recursive search temporarily changes a working board to explore alternatives, which must not silently become the player's actual move. The documented Rust search makes a copy at its outer entry, while its in-place search relies on restoration of the working board [6]. Cloning the root board once per search request isolates exploratory tree mutations from the live game state, while in-place apply and undo avoid O(N²) board copying at internal nodes.
new: Board mutation and match progression have separate owners. Board holds the cells and move count; Game and the frontend controller maintain turn, result and history. Search explores hypothetical moves on a working board, while the match commits only the selected move. The modified Rust search clones the root board once and applies and undoes moves within that copy [6]. This avoids a complete board copy for each child, although candidate generation still allocates move lists at internal nodes.
reason: Clarifies actual root-copy/in-place ownership and counters earlier zero-allocation claim.

old: For example, let X occupy (7,7), O occupy (8,7), and the count be two. Trying X at (7,8) changes that cell and makes the count three. Undoing (7,8) returns both the cells and count to their initial values. Clearing the cell but leaving count three makes fullness checks unreliable; decrementing without clearing contaminates the next branch. With direct indexing, each operation is O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space; copying an N × N board costs O(N²). Rejecting an occupied or out-of-bounds move must leave the board unchanged. Together with the inductive restoration invariant, automated root-restoration checks across 820 engine search runs confirm that the working board is returned unchanged after every search.

old: Inputs, outputs and preconditions. The procedure takes a board and the last placed coordinate m, and returns the winner and a collection of winning cells when a qualifying line is found, or no result otherwise. It assumes m refers to the move that may have just caused the transition. If the board was already won before that move, testing only a line through m cannot detect every earlier win. A root-level validation of an arbitrary imported board needs a separate full-board check. The current frontend rule reads the player at m; an empty or invalid location produces no winner.
new: The procedure receives a valid board and the last placed coordinate m. It returns the winning player and collected winning cells, or no result. It assumes the preceding position was unfinished, so any newly created winning line passes through m. An arbitrary imported position instead requires a full-board result check at the search root. Under the frontend state contract, an empty last-move coordinate yields no winner [4].
reason: Clarifies valid-board precondition rather than asserting WinRule itself validates arbitrary invalid state.

old: Consider X X [X] X X on one row with the bracketed center as the last move. Each side contributes two; 1+2+2=5. For X X X [X] X X, the value exceeds five and remains a win. An empty last cell returns no winner; a gap interrupts the run; edge and corner scans stop safely. Why last-move 4-axis ray scanning is used: because any newly formed winning line in an ongoing game must pass through the stone m just placed, scanning at most K − 1 = 4 steps in both directions (+1 and −1) along the 4 axes D = {(1,0), (0,1), (1,1), (1,−1)} inspects at most 4 × 2 × 4 = 32 neighboring cells. Benefits and trade-offs: this reduces terminal win detection at every recursive search node from an O(N²) full-board scan (225 × 4 = 900 directional checks) to O(K) = O(1) time and O(K) space, yielding a major speedup inside Minimax and Alpha-Beta; the trade-off is that it relies on the inductive invariant that no prior move had already won, so arbitrary imported positions require a one-time O(N²) root validation.
new: For X X [X] X X on a row, with the bracketed cell placed last, each side contributes two stones and 1 + 2 + 2 = 5. For X X X [X] X X, the run exceeds five and is still a win. A gap or board edge stops the corresponding scan. With K = 5, the frontend examines at most 4 × 2 × 4 = 32 neighboring positions, giving O(K) time and O(K) space for the collected cells. These bounds are constant for the configured winning length. A full-board scan checks every occupied starting point and has a different cost; the report does not infer an elapsed-time speedup from the operation count alone.
reason: Removes unmeasured major-speedup claim and invalid exact comparison to 900 full-board checks; keeps derivation.

In the modified Rust snapshot, Easy first rejects an empty player or terminal board, enumerates empty cells, and selects an index using a seeded 64-bit mixer modulo the list length. It evaluates the chosen move afterwards to populate the result; that evaluation does not influence selection [6].

old: The input includes the seed because pseudo-random generation is deterministic for a particular generator state and input. The output is either an element of L or no move. With a board containing only one stone, |L|=224; a one-element list always returns its sole entry. A full or terminal board must not perform modulo zero. The legality argument is immediate from construction of L, provided the game-level preconditions and list are correct. Using a deterministic 64-bit splitmix-style mixer over the legal move list ensures fast O(1) index selection after O(N²) empty-cell enumeration.
new: The seed is part of the input because the mixer is deterministic. The output is a member of L or no move. A board with one stone has 224 empty cells, while a one-element list always returns its sole coordinate. Terminal handling precedes modulo selection, so a full board cannot cause division by zero. Index selection takes O(1) after enumeration. Modulo reduction does not in general produce an exactly uniform distribution over arbitrary list lengths.
reason: Corrects exact-uniformity implication and explains selection safely without marketing claims.

old: The publicly archived Rust baseline defines the following weights for two open ends and one open end, respectively: length at least five, 1,000,000 and 1,000,000; length four, 50,000 and 5,000; length three, 5,000 and 500; and length two, 200 and 50. A run of five or more has the same weight even when both ends are closed; otherwise unmatched cases receive zero from the run-weight function [15]. Why exponential pattern weights are used: scaling weights by an order of magnitude per stone—from 50/200 for two-stone runs to 500/5,000 for three-stone runs, 5,000/50,000 for four-stone runs, and 1,000,000 for five-or-more—ensures that an unstoppable open four (50,000) or double-three threat decisively outweighs multiple scattered two-stone formations, while the Manhattan center term c(x,y) = max(0, 14 − |x − 7| − |y − 7|) breaks positional ties in the opening.
new: The archived evaluator assigns weights of 1,000,000 to a run of at least five; 50,000 or 5,000 to a four with two or one open ends; 5,000 or 500 to a three; and 200 or 50 to a two. A run of five or more receives the same weight even with closed ends. Other cases receive zero [15]. These manually chosen weights favour longer, open formations, while the center term adds a smaller positional preference. They are heuristic parameters, rather than a proof that a named threat always outweighs every combination of shorter runs.
reason: Removes false exponential progression, unsupported double-three modelling and unconditional tactical dominance.

old: The loop invariant is that score equals the signed contribution of all starts already visited, plus center terms for occupied cells already visited. Every maximal run has exactly one start in each orientation, so the preceding-cell test avoids counting that run repeatedly. Because every maximal contiguous run has a unique starting cell along each axis, the preceding-cell guard (skipping cell s when s − d holds the same color) guarantees that each run is weighted exactly once per axis without double-counting sub-segments.
new: After each visited run start, score contains the signed run contributions processed so far and the center contributions of previously visited occupied cells. The preceding-cell guard skips interior stones of the same run. Every maximal run therefore contributes once per axis, even when it contains several stones.
reason: Removes duplicated invariant proof while preserving exact claim.

old: For an illustrative board with X alone at (7,7), its singleton has no run weight and its center term is 14, so E(B,X)=14. Add X at (8,7) while leaving the remainder empty: the horizontal length-two run has two open ends and contributes 200; center terms are 14 and 13, so the value is 227. A blocked endpoint reduces open(r) from 2 to 1 (or 0 when blocked on both sides), shifting the run weight down by an order of magnitude; board boundaries act as closed endpoints.

Adding X at (8,7) creates an open horizontal two worth 200; the center terms are 14 and 13, giving 227. For a run shorter than five, changing an empty endpoint to an occupied endpoint changes its open-end classification and corresponding weight. A board boundary also closes an endpoint.

old: Scanning all maximal runs across a constant number of directions is O(N²): although a run is traversed, each occupied cell participates in at most one maximal run per direction. Auxiliary space beyond the board is O(1) in the described scan. The evaluator recognizes contiguous runs; a gap such as XX_XX is not automatically a single contiguous run, even though a separate move test can recognize the winning gap. Benefits and trade-offs of maximal contiguous-run scanning: it evaluates any board in O(N²) time and O(1) auxiliary memory without dynamic allocation; the trade-off is that single-gap threats (such as XX_XX) are not scored as a single contiguous run at depth 0, relying instead on multi-ply look-ahead recursion and the candidate generator's tactical assessment to resolve split completions.
new: Scanning maximal runs in four directions takes O(N²) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond the board: each occupied cell belongs to at most one maximal run per direction. This evaluator counts contiguous runs. A split formation such as XX_XX is represented as separate runs at the horizon, although candidate assessment can identify the empty gap as a winning completion. Thus horizon evaluation and tactical move assessment capture different properties of the position.
reason: Removes repetitive benefits/trade-off template and unsupported implication deeper search always resolves split threat.

The result from root perspective is M−q for a root win, −M+q for a root loss, and zero for a draw. An unfinished board has no terminal utility and is evaluated only when the search horizon is reached [6].

A root win returns M − q, a root loss returns −M + q, and a draw returns zero. Nonterminal evaluations are clamped to the closed interval [−H,H], where H = M − 225 − 1 = 99,999,774 [6].

old: The membership invariant says that each appended coordinate is on the board, empty and not previously appended. Conversely, every empty cell in a visited neighborhood is appended on its first encounter. This proves correctness for the defined neighborhood, not equivalence to all legal moves. With m occupied cells, scanning the board and their neighborhoods costs O(N² + m(2r+1)²) before assessment; the seen matrix and candidate list use O(N²) space. The domain can be clipped at the board edge. Benefits and trade-offs of Chebyshev spatial pruning: restricting moves to d∞(a,b) = max(|a_x − b_x|, |a_y − b_y|) ≤ r reduces the branching factor from ~220 empty cells in the opening to 8–36 local candidates (a 72.39%–83.64% reduction), making multi-ply search tractable; the trade-off is that distant non-local sacrifices outside radius r are excluded from the search tree.
new: Each appended coordinate is in bounds, empty and previously unseen. Conversely, every empty cell in a visited neighborhood is appended on its first encounter. This establishes membership in the radius policy. With m occupied cells, board scanning and neighborhood enumeration take O(N² + m(2r + 1)²) time before assessment; the seen matrix and move list use O(N²) space. The policy reduces the set searched, but can exclude legal moves outside the chosen neighborhood.
reason: Removes arithmetically inconsistent 8–36/72.39–83.64% comparison and unmeasured tractability claim.

old: For k raw candidates, assessment takes O(kK) when the relevant directional scan is bounded by K, sorting O(k log k), and storage O(k), in addition to spatial generation. With fixed K=5 the scan term is linear in k. Candidate assessment and full-board evaluation are different operations; a counter named ordering evaluations should be interpreted using its own recorded definition. Why a soft tactical cap C' = T ∪ Top_max(0, c − |T|)(C \ T) is used instead of a hard cap: a hard truncation at cap c can discard critical winning or blocking moves if their static heuristic rank falls below index c—as demonstrated in the cap_loss.json benchmark where a hard cap of 6 discarded both winning endpoints (7,2) and (7,7) out of 20 candidates. By taking max(cap, 1, tactical_count), the soft cap guarantees 100% retention of immediate 1-ply wins and blocks (T) while bounding non-tactical branching to at most c candidates [16].
new: For k raw candidates, bounded directional assessment takes O(kK), sorting takes O(k log k), and move storage takes O(k), in addition to neighborhood generation. Let C be the raw set, T its assessed win-or-block subset, and c the normalized cap. Selection retains T plus the highest-ranked non-tactical moves needed to reach c, when available. Its total size is min(|C|, max(c, |T|)); it can exceed c. The separate native reference experiment in cap_loss.json illustrates the danger of a hard cap: cap 6 retained six of twenty candidates and omitted both winning endpoints. That result concerns the reference policy, while the modified policy preserves every assessed member of T [16].
reason: Fixes cap semantics, bounds tactical guarantee and separates reference hard-cap failure from modified engine.

old: For example, if A, B and C have quick ranking scores 10, 50 and 30, score order is B, C, A, while coordinate order may be A, B, C. Neither order establishes that B is ultimately the best move. If all are still visited under minimax, only traversal changes. Alpha-beta may finish earlier after B supplies a strong bound. Sorting k moves costs O(k log k), plus the cost of computing keys and O(k) storage in a conventional array implementation. Benefits and trade-offs of move ordering: examining immediate wins, blocks, and high-adjacency moves first maximizes early α ≥ β cutoffs and reduces visited nodes by 44.68%–80.22% in depth-2 benchmarks; the trade-off is the O(k log k) sorting and key-assessment overhead at each node, which must remain lightweight so ranking cost does not exceed pruning savings.

old: Why the six difficulty tiers are divided this way: the configuration table is designed around two mathematical principles. First, it separates qualitative decision regimes: Easy (d = 0, Random across all empty cells) provides a non-tactical baseline for beginners; Normal (d = 1, uncapped local neighborhood) introduces 1-ply immediate win/block priority and static heuristic scoring; and Hard through Master (d = 2 to 5, Chebyshev radius r = 2) engage multi-ply Alpha-Beta look-ahead. Second, across the four Alpha-Beta tiers, search depth increases linearly (d = 2, 3, 4, 5) while the soft candidate cap tightens inversely (c = 15, 12, 10, 8). Because an adversarial tree with branching factor c and depth d scales as O(c^d) in the worst case (and O(c^(d/2)) under ideal Alpha-Beta ordering), keeping c = 15 at d = 5 would expand up to 15^5 = 759,375 nodes per turn. Tightening the soft cap to c = 8 bounds the worst-case tree to 8^5 = 32,768 nodes (and ~2,000–5,000 nodes with Alpha-Beta pruning), keeping Web Worker latency within interactive browser budgets (47, 252, 551, and 1,418 visited nodes in 1.1–3.0 ms on the benchmarked midgame fixture). Benefits and trade-offs: this inverse (d, c) scaling delivers smooth skill progression and responsive UI performance while the soft tactical cap max(c, 1, |T|) and frontend tactical prepass guarantee that zero immediate 1-ply wins or blocks are ever dropped; the trade-off is that deeper tiers (Expert, Master) prune lower-ranked quiet positional candidates (ranked below index 10 or 8) in exchange for deeper 4-to-5-ply tactical calculation.

The remaining tiers use alpha-beta at depths 2–5 with radius 2 and nominal caps 15, 12, 10 and 8. Reducing the nominal width offsets some of the growth from increased depth, but these are soft caps: assessed wins and blocks can increase the retained set. For illustration, a uniform tree of width 8 and depth 5 has 8^5 = 32,768 leaves and 37,449 total nodes before pruning. This is a fixed-width model, not an upper bound for the implemented soft-cap search. The tier timings and actual counters are reported in Chapter 5; configuration alone does not establish a latency bound or a measured progression in playing strength.
